topic: Bill of exchange and promissory note
question: Distinguish between a bill of exchange and a promissory note.
sources: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Section 4 (promissory note) and Section 5 (bill of exchange)
Standard accounting treatment of bills of exchange

points.label: Nature of instrument
points.description: A promissory note contains an unconditional promise by the maker to pay; a bill of exchange contains an unconditional order by the drawer directing the drawee to pay.

points.label: Number of parties
points.description: A promissory note has two parties, the maker and the payee; a bill has three, the drawer, the drawee and the payee (though drawer and payee may be the same person).
points.basis: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, Sections 4 and 5 and parties to the instruments

points.label: Acceptance
points.description: A promissory note needs no acceptance because the maker himself promises to pay; a bill must be accepted by the drawee before it binds him.
points.basis: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, acceptance of a bill by the drawee

points.label: Liability of maker or drawer
points.description: The maker of a note is primarily and unconditionally liable; the drawer of a bill is liable only secondarily, if the drawee (acceptor) fails to pay.
points.basis: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, liability of maker, drawer and acceptor

points.label: Notice of dishonour
points.description: On dishonour of a note, notice to the maker is not needed; on dishonour of a bill, notice must be given to the drawer and indorsers to hold them liable.
points.basis: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881, notice of dishonour
